eras.label: The officials' Storting
eras.blurb: Norway kept its own constitution and parliament through the union with Sweden, and elected them in two stages: voters chose electors, electors chose members. The franchise reached farmers who owned their land, townsmen of property and public officials, which in practice was a few per cent of the population, and no parties existed to organise any of it. Almost every member on this page is listed as an independent because that is what they were.

eras.label: Parliamentarism and the union's end
eras.blurb: The impeachment of the Selmer cabinet in 1884 established that a Norwegian government answers to the Storting rather than to the king in Stockholm, and Venstre and Høyre were founded within weeks of each other to fight over it. Universal male suffrage arrived in 1898 and turnout promptly passed 80%. The union with Sweden was dissolved in 1905 and women received the vote in 1913.

eras.label: Between the wars
eras.blurb: Proportional representation replaced single-member districts in 1921 and the Storting fragmented at once. Labour grew from a revolutionary party that had joined the Comintern into the largest in the country, took office briefly in 1928, and returned in 1935 on a crisis pact with the Agrarians that ended a decade of minority governments.

eras.label: Labour's long ascendancy
eras.blurb: Labour governed alone for the twenty years after the occupation, holding an absolute majority of seats at six consecutive elections, and built the Norwegian welfare state while doing it. The EEC referendum of 1972 split the country along a line that has never quite closed, and the oil began to arrive in the same decade.

eras.label: The four-party system and after
eras.blurb: Labour's majorities went and did not come back. The Progress Party turned tax and immigration into a permanent bloc on the right, the Centre Party carried rural Norway against Europe in a second referendum in 1994, and government became a matter of assembling three or four parties rather than winning.

eras.label: The present Storting
eras.blurb: Erna Solberg's right-wing coalition held for eight years, Labour's Jonas Gahr Støre took it back in 2021 and lost his Centre Party partner over energy prices in 2025. That September the Progress Party finished second with 47 seats, its best result, and Labour was returned as a minority government all the same.
